title: Three noun genders
goal: Face the most typical rule of Icelandic: every noun — including table, chair, and book — has a gender, and that gender decides the form of the adjectives and pronouns that go with it.
bekal: name the gender of a noun and guess it from the word's ending
use *hann*, *hún*, and *það* for **things**, not just for people

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Í kennslustofunni
dialogs.intro: In the classroom. Anna holds up a few objects and points to them one by one; Búdí has just discovered the rule that confuses him most.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Rétt. Bókin er ný. Hún er líka dýr.
lines.id: Right. The book is new. It's also expensive.
lines.literal: right. book-the is new. she is also expensive.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.id: "She"? But the book isn't a woman!
lines.literal: she? but book-the is not woman!

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Nei, en bók er kvenkyn. Þess vegna segjum við „hún".
lines.id: No, but bók is feminine. That's why we say "hún".
lines.literal: no, but book is feminine-gender. that's why say we she.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Þá er þetta erfitt. Hvað með borðið?
lines.id: Then this is hard. What about the table?
lines.literal: then is this hard. what with table-the?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Borð er hvorugkyn. Þess vegna: það er stórt og það er brúnt.
lines.id: Borð is neuter. So: it's big and it's brown.
lines.literal: table is neuter-gender. that's why: it is big and it is brown.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Stóll er karlkyn. Hann er nýr og hann er þægilegur.
lines.id: Stóll is masculine. It's new and it's comfortable.
lines.literal: chair is masculine-gender. he is new and he is comfortable.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Svo hver hlutur hefur kyn? Hvernig veit ég það?
lines.id: So every object has a gender? How do I know?
lines.literal: so every object has gender? how know I it?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Endingin segir þér það oftast. Ekki hafa áhyggjur — þú lærir þetta smám saman.
lines.id: The ending usually tells you. Don't worry — you'll learn it little by little.
lines.literal: ending-the says to-you it most-often. not have worries — you learn this small-by-small together.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Gott. Þá er bókin mín kvenkyn og stóllinn minn karlkyn!
lines.id: Good. Then my book is feminine and my chair is masculine!
lines.literal: good. then is book-the mine feminine and chair-the mine masculine!

notes: **Hann and hún are used for THINGS, not just for people.** This is the biggest shift in thinking in the whole course. *Bókin? Hún er ný.* — "The book? **She**'s new." Translating it as "she" feels odd in English, and it should: what's marked is not maleness or femaleness but a **grammatical class**. In normal English you simply say "it".

**The three genders have plain, honest names**: *karlkyn* (masculine, abbreviated **kk**), *kvenkyn* (feminine, **kvk**), *hvorugkyn* (neuter, **hk**). Icelandic dictionaries always print these abbreviations next to the noun, so get used to reading them now.

**Þetta and það both mean "this/that", but they aren't interchangeable.** *Þetta* is used when you **point at** something new to the conversation: *Hvað er þetta?* *Það* is used for something **already** mentioned, or as "it": *Það er bók.*

**The adjective changes form too, and that's not optional.** *Nýr* for kk, *ný* for kvk, *nýtt* for hk — and the same pattern holds for almost all adjectives. This is the main reason you need to know a noun's gender: without it, you can't choose the adjective form.

**Ekki hafa áhyggjur — a negative command.** Literally "don't have worries". Notice that *ekki* stands at the very front of a command, the only place where it comes before its verb. Commands are covered in full in Unit 13.

**Smám saman means "little by little", and it's serious advice.** No Icelander memorizes genders from a list; they learn each noun **together with its article** — not *bók* but *bókin*. Do the same from Unit 4 on.

grammars.title: Three genders and their pronouns
body: What decides is not the meaning of the word but its form. *Kona* (woman) is indeed kvenkyn, but *skip* (ship) is hvorugkyn and *bíll* (car) is karlkyn for no reason you could put your finger on.
after: ⚠️ Note that *barn* (child) is **neuter**, neither masculine nor feminine — so even a little boy is *það* if the word used is *barn*. Only with *strákur* (boy) do you say *hann*.
The plural has its own pronouns: *þeir* (kk), *þær* (kvk), *þau* (hk **and** mixed). A family of a father and a mother is always *þau*, because it's mixed.

grammars.title: Adjectives follow the noun's gender
body: The ending pattern repeats across almost all adjectives: **-ur / — / -t**. Memorize the pattern, not each word.
after: The **hk** form almost always ends in **-t**, and that's the most useful clue: if you hear an adjective ending in -t, the word it describes is almost certainly neuter.

When there's no clear noun — for example when describing a situation or the weather — Icelandic uses the **hk** form: *það er gott*, *það er kalt*, *þetta er erfitt*. Neuter is the language's default form.

sections.title: Guessing the gender from the ending

blocks.text: No rule works a hundred percent of the time, but there are tendencies that cover most everyday words. Use them as a first guess, not as law.

blocks.title: A way of memorizing that really works
items: Never memorize a bare noun. Learn it **with its article**: not *bók* but **bókin**, not *borð* but **borðið**, not *stóll* but **stóllinn**. The ending itself tells you the gender, so you learn two things at once with no extra effort.
This also explains why the next unit goes straight to the article: it isn't a separate grammar chapter but a **memory tool** for the rest of this course.

sections.title: Things around you, with their genders

blocks.text: You'll use these twelve words again and again in Units 4 to 12. Say each one with its pronoun — *stóll, hann*; *bók, hún*; *borð, það* — until the pairs stick without thinking.

exercises.prompt: Give the gender of each noun: kk, kvk, or hk.
Replace the noun with the right pronoun: *hann*, *hún*, or *það*.
items: Bókin er ný. ____ er líka dýr.
Blaðið er gamalt. ____ er ekki gott.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form of the adjective.

items: The book is new and expensive.
The house is small but good.

answers: kk — kvk — hk — kvk — hk — kk
nýr — stór — gott — dýr — fallegt — lítil
Hvað er þetta? — Það er bók. — Bókin er ný og dýr. — Borðið er stórt. — Stóllinn er þægilegur. — Húsið er lítið en gott.
